Can a balcony solar system run a no-install split air conditioner?

Solar basics Updated 2026-08-03

Not directly. The two balcony batteries in this library each discharge 1,200 W, while the air conditioner’s own maker declares a nameplate ceiling of 1,500 W and 7 A — so the compatibility engine refuses both pairings on continuous output, at 125% of what the battery can supply.

A portable power station is a different answer: 5 of the 14 published EU records here clear the same load outright and 2 come back marginal. How long any of them holds it is a question nobody can answer yet, and what is missing is a duty cycle rather than a battery.

Open the runtime calculator →

Policy content, and what its date means

Nothing here states what may be connected at your address. Balcony-generation rules differ by grid operator and by country and are amended frequently; this page names where their text lives and restates no threshold from any of them.

Wording checked 2026-08-03 · next review due 2027-01-30 · scope: the two manufacturers’ declared output ceilings quoted on this page, read off their own product records, and the query path handed to the reader in place of an answer

Why these two products end up on the same balcony

Neither product has a US counterpart, and both are bought by the same person: a tenant who may not drill the wall and may not touch the meter cupboard. The air conditioner is a split unit whose indoor and outdoor halves join through a flat hose passing under a closed window — no hole, no installer, no refrigerant work on site. The balcony battery is a storage product built around a registration regime, sold with a plug on a cable; this library holds two, both EU-only. The appliance record’s US profile is switched off for a matching reason: its figures come from a 230 V manual, and the US certification dataset this site reads describes nothing of this shape.

What a balcony inverter can actually hand over

The two balcony records, and the load put in front of them

Each of these products publishes two different output numbers, and they are not interchangeable: what the battery discharges into the flat, and what it pushes back through the meter. This pairing is decided by the first.

Both makers state a feed-in ceiling alongside — not instead of — the discharge rating, and both records carry it on the AC-output field, official tier, checked 2026-08-01. It is the manufacturers’ own declared product ceiling. This site has not read the enacted text behind it and states nothing about what any reader is permitted to do.

Official spec + Derived by WattPair · verified 2026-08-01 · balcony storage records · EU

The comparison finishes before the export question is reached. 1,500 W against 1,200 W leaves the balcony battery short by a quarter on the only path that matters — running an appliance in your own flat is a discharge, not an export, and the feed-in ceiling governs the other direction. That distinction is missing from most of the discussion this question generates, and it is why a bigger array fixes nothing.

Why a station rated at exactly the nameplate watts still fails

An inverter is rated in watts and has to supply volt-amperes. The maker declares both on one nameplate line, and at 230 V the current side is larger.

Apparent power at the nameplate point 1,610 VA Derived from official coefficients · verified 2026-08-03 · medium confidence

The declared 7 A at nominal mains voltage: more than a 1,500 W inverter is rated to supply, even though the watts match exactly.

The instant it starts, which no document describes

The start-up fields, as both inverter records carry them

Every verdict here was decided on the running load, because we have found the quantity that usually decides an air-conditioner verdict in no document from either maker.

The no-install split — start-up, as a multiple Not found in the sources we checked no figure to date

The maker’s German manual carries the most complete electrical table in this library — watts and amps for rated cooling, rated heating and the nameplate ceiling — and nothing at all for the start. The EU product database does not ask split units for it either, so the absence is structural rather than an oversight.

The US inverter window unit — the same field Not found in the sources we checked no figure to date

The same finding on the other side of the Atlantic, on a different appliance class under a different regulator. Two legal systems, two document sets, one empty field.

The engine treats that gap as a constraint it cannot judge rather than as a zero — a disclosure, not a reassurance. A balcony battery refused at 125% would not be rescued by a start-up figure arriving, and a station that clears the running load has not thereby been shown to survive the start.

The rules, and the sentence we will not write

What this page does not tell you

Whether you may connect any of this to anything at your address. A balcony system’s export ceiling, its registration duty and who may make the connection are set by your grid operator’s rules and by national law, all of which move. This page restates no threshold from any of them. The feed-in figure quoted here is what two manufacturers declare about their own products, checked 2026-08-03 — evidence of the shape they are built to, not permission.

Where the answer for your own address lives

Four documents, none of which this site can read for you. Stop at the first no.

1
Your grid operator’s connection rules

The operator of the network your meter hangs on publishes what may be connected behind it, and under what conditions. The document that decides most cases.

2
Your national registry for small generating plant

Most European markets require a small generating system to be registered, sometimes with a simplified process below a threshold. Read the rule’s current text, not a retailer’s summary of it.

3
Your lease, or your building’s owners’ association

Anything clamped to a railing is visible from outside and usually has a clause about it. A statutory exemption instructs a grid operator; it does not rewrite a private contract.

4
In the United States, the same question splits into four

State statute, utility interconnection rules, the adopted electrical code and your lease, with the enacted bills named one at a time.

How long will it run, and why we will not say

Run the pairing that clears every constraint and the engine still declines to print hours. It reports how fast the load consumes energy and names what it is missing: the portable split air conditioner (hose-through-window) record’s own load.duty_cycle. The gate is on the appliance, not the battery — the same station prints hours happily for a fridge.

The two energy figures that exist, and what each is for

Both official, both correct, and answering different questions. That distance is the size of the thing we found no measurement of.

Annual energy, as declared to the EU 135 kWh Official spec · verified 2026-08-03 · high confidence

For the cooling-only model of the same product line, from its EU product-database entry. A whole-season figure with a legally defined method behind it.

See the load record →
Season-average electrical power implied by that figure 386 W Derived by WattPair

The regulation defines annual consumption as the design cooling load times 350 equivalent operating hours divided by the seasonal efficiency ratio. Running that identity backwards on the record’s own annual figure gives the average power the label implies, and it is computed on this build from that field alone. It is an average across a whole season, part-load hours included, which is why the record forbids its use for outage runtime.

Duty cycle Not found in the sources we checked no figure to date

Deliberately empty, and deliberately not borrowed. Every cycling figure this library holds for an air conditioner describes a fixed-speed machine that stops and restarts; a variable-speed unit slows down instead, so multiplying its rated watts by a fixed-speed machine’s on-time fraction produces a quantity that does not exist.

Official spec + Derived by WattPair · verified 2026-08-03 · no-install split AC · energy fields

Those two figures bracket the truth from opposite sides, and an honest conservative estimate uses the bracket rather than a point inside it. Divide a battery by the nameplate ceiling and you get a floor on the hours: true, and pessimistic by an unknown margin, since the compressor spends most of its life below that ceiling. Divide by the season average instead and the answer flatters you by roughly 4×, because that average already contains every part-load hour of a cooling season. Plan against the floor, and note that a maker’s stated outdoor operating range — not the battery — is what ends the conversation in a real heatwave.

What would unlock an hour figure here

One first-hand measurement of how a variable-speed room air conditioner modulates — a duty cycle, or a power curve against room temperature, from a source we can name and date. The record already names the missing field and carries the gate that reads it. Until such a source exists this site prints the consumption rate and stops there.

Questions people ask

Can a balcony solar system run an air conditioner?
Not the no-install split unit this page is written against, and the panels are not the reason. Both balcony batteries in our library discharge 1,200 W into the flat, and the appliance’s maker declares a 1,500 W nameplate ceiling, so the engine refuses both pairings on continuous output. The separate feed-in ceiling these products carry governs export, which is the other direction and not how a battery runs a load in your own home.
Can a portable power station run a PortaSplit-style no-install split AC?
Several can, on the running load. A station has to hold 1,500 W continuously and 1,610 VA of apparent power, and it is the volt-ampere figure that catches a machine rated at exactly 1,500 W. What no station can be shown to do is start it, because we have found no published start-up current for a variable-speed compressor.
How much electricity does a no-install split air conditioner use?
The cooling-only model declares 135 kWh a year to the EU product database, and its rated cooling draw is 1,230 W against a 1,500 W nameplate ceiling. Those answer different questions and must not be combined: the annual figure is computed over a defined season including part-load hours, and the nameplate is an instantaneous ceiling. We have found nothing published that would connect them — how the machine modulates between the two.
